habitat: Rabbitfish inhabit coral reefs and lagoons of the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to French Polynesia and the Great Barrier Reef. They are found at depths of 1-30 meters, frequenting outer reef slopes, seagrass beds, and protected lagoons. They are diurnal, spending daylight hours foraging and seeking shelter among coral branches and rock crevices at night. Their compressed, oval body shape allows them to navigate through narrow coral passages with ease.
diet: Rabbitfish are primarily herbivorous, feeding on various species of algae including macroalgae and turf algae growing on rocks and dead coral. They play a vital ecological role in controlling algal growth that competes with corals for space on reefs. They also consume seagrass and occasionally sponges. Their rabbit-like mouth (hence the name) has specialized teeth for scraping algae. In captivity, they eagerly accept nori, spirulina, and fresh vegetables.
behavior: Rabbitfish are peaceful schooling fish that rely on numbers for safety. When threatened, they erect their venomous dorsal, anal, and pelvic spines as a formidable defense. Their venom causes painful stings (mild to moderate pain in humans) but is not life-threatening. They undergo dramatic color changes — shifting from bright daytime patterns to mottled, darker camouflage at night or when stressed. Some species sleep in mucus cocoons that mask their scent from predators.
facts: Rabbitfish get their name from their rabbit-like snout and herbivorous grazing behavior. All rabbitfish have venomous fin spines — 13 dorsal, 7 anal, and 4 pelvic — each grooved with venom glands. They are important food fish across Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands. Their color-changing ability is among the most dramatic of any reef fish. There are approximately 29 recognized species in the Siganus genus. They are closely related to surgeonfish and can grow 25-40 cm.
naming: Rabbitfish names might reflect their rabbit-like appearance or reef habitat. Consider names like Bunny, Algae, Reef, Nori, Spike (for their venomous spines), Lagoon, Thorn, Herby, Coral, or Siganus.
